blocks.body: To study primes $p\equiv a\pmod q$ we need to pick out one residue class from all integers. The indicator function of "$n\equiv a\pmod q$" is periodic but not multiplicative, so it has no Euler product. Dirichlet's idea (1837) was to write that indicator as a linear combination of periodic functions that are completely multiplicative. These are the characters. Each has its own $L$-function with an Euler product, and analysing those $L$-functions is how Dirichlet proved that every progression $a, a+q, a+2q,\dots$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$ contains infinitely many primes.

blocks.title: A first example: modulo 4
blocks.body:
The odd numbers split into $n\equiv1$ and $n\equiv3\pmod4$. Define $\chi_0(n)=1$ for odd $n$, and $\chi_1(n)=(-1)^{(n-1)/2}$, which is $+1$ on $1\bmod4$ and $-1$ on $3\bmod4$. Both vanish on even $n$. Both are completely multiplicative: for $\chi_1$, this is the fact that the product of two numbers $\equiv3\pmod 4$ is $\equiv1\pmod4$. And
$$\frac{\chi_0(n)+\chi_1(n)}2=\begin{cases}1&n\equiv1\pmod4\\0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad \frac{\chi_0(n)-\chi_1(n)}2=\begin{cases}1&n\equiv3\pmod4\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
So "primes $\equiv1\pmod 4$" can be studied through the two multiplicative functions $\chi_0$ and $\chi_1$. The general theory does exactly this for every modulus.

blocks.title: Dirichlet character
How many characters there are
blocks.body: There are exactly $\varphi(q)$ characters modulo $q$. Under pointwise multiplication they form a group, with identity $\chi_0$ and inverse $\bar\chi$. Moreover, if $\gcd(n,q)=1$ and $n\not\equiv1\pmod q$, then some character has $\chi(n)\ne1$.

Cyclic case first. If $(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^	imes$ is cyclic, say generated by a primitive root $g$ of order $m=\varphi(q)$ ([[order-primroot]]), then a character is determined by $\chi(g)$. That value must satisfy $\chi(g)^m=1$, and each of the $m$ choices $\chi(g)=e^{2\pi ik/m}$ gives a well-defined character $\chi(g^e)=e^{2\pi ike/m}$. If $n=g^e$ with $e

General case. By the [[crt]], $(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^	imes$ is the product of the groups $(\mathbb Z/p^k\mathbb Z)^	imes$ over $p^k\parallel q$. For odd $p$ these are cyclic. For $p=2$: the group is trivial for $k=1$, cyclic of order $2$ for $k=2$, and for $k\ge3$ every odd $n$ is uniquely $\pm5^e$ with $0\le e<2^{k-2}$. So there are generators $g_1,\dots,g_r$ of orders $m_1,\dots,m_r$, with $m_1\cdots m_r=\varphi(q)$, such that every unit is uniquely $g_1^{e_1}\cdots g_r^{e_r}$ with $e_j$ taken mod $m_j$. A character is then determined freely by choosing each $\chi(g_j)$ among the $m_j$-th roots of unity. Every choice is well defined, by the uniqueness of the exponents. blocks.title: Orthogonality relations
blocks.body:
1. $\displaystyle\sum_{n\bmod q}\chi(n)=\begin{cases}\varphi(q)&\chi=\chi_0\\0&\chi\ne\chi_0.\end{cases}$

2. $\displaystyle\sum_{\chi\bmod q}\chi(n)=\begin{cases}\varphi(q)&n\equiv1\pmod q\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$

3. If $\gcd(a,q)=1$, then
$$\frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi \bmod q} \overline{\chi}(a)\,\chi(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n \equiv a \pmod q\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

1. If $\chi\ne\chi_0$, pick $m$ coprime to $q$ with $\chi(m)\ne1$. As $n$ runs over residues mod $q$, so does $mn$. Hence $S=\sum\chi(mn)=\chi(m)S$, which forces $S=0$.

2. If $\gcd(n,q)>1$, every term is $0$. If $\gcd(n,q)=1$ and $n\not\equiv1$, the theorem gives $\psi$ with $\psi(n)\ne1$. Since $\chi\mapsto\psi\chi$ permutes the characters, $T=\sum_\chi\psi(n)\chi(n)=\psi(n)T$, so $T=0$.

3. Let $\bar a$ be an inverse of $a$ mod $q$ ([[mod-inverse]]). Since $|\chi(a)|=1$, we have $\overline{\chi}(a)=\chi(a)^{-1}=\chi(\bar a)$. So the sum is $\sum_\chi\chi(\bar an)$, and by 2 this is $\varphi(q)$ if $\bar an\equiv1$, that is if $n\equiv a$, and $0$ otherwise.

blocks.title: Picking out a progression
blocks.body:
Relation 3 is the whole point. For any function $f$ and any $a$ coprime to $q$,
$$\sum_{\substack{p\le x\\p\equiv a\ (q)}}f(p)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}\overline\chi(a)\sum_{p\le x}\chi(p)f(p).$$
The principal character contributes $\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{p\le x,\,p\nmid q}f(p)$, the same for every $a$. This is the expected main term, with the primes shared equally among the $\varphi(q)$ classes. Every other character contributes a sum $\sum\chi(p)f(p)$ with oscillating weights, which one hopes is smaller. Showing that it really is smaller is where $L(s,\chi)=\sum\chi(n)n^{-s}$ and the fact $L(1,\chi)\ne0$ enter ([[l-functions]]).

Some vocabulary. A character is real if all its values are real, so they lie in $\{0,\pm1\}$; this happens exactly when $\chi^2=\chi_0$. For an odd prime $p$, the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ ([[quadratic-residues]]) is the unique real character mod $p$ other than $\chi_0$. Since $\chi(-1)^2=\chi(1)=1$, every character is even ($\chi(-1)=1$) or odd ($\chi(-1)=-1$).

blocks.title: Induced and primitive characters
blocks.body:
Let $d\mid q$ and let $\chi^*$ be a character mod $d$. The character $\chi$ mod $q$ defined by $\chi(n)=\chi^*(n)$ for $\gcd(n,q)=1$ (and $0$ otherwise) is said to be induced by $\chi^*$. The conductor of $\chi$ is the least $d\mid q$ such that $\chi$ is induced from a character mod $d$. The character $\chi$ is primitive if its conductor is $q$ itself.

A practical test: $\chi$ is induced from modulus $d$ if and only if $\chi(n)=1$ whenever $n\equiv1\pmod d$ and $\gcd(n,q)=1$. One direction is clear. For the other, reduction mod $d$ maps $(\mathbb Z/q)^\times$ onto $(\mathbb Z/d)^\times$ (by the [[crt]]), and a homomorphism that is trivial on the kernel factors through the quotient.

blocks.title: Counting cube roots with characters
blocks.body: Let $p$ be a prime and $p\nmid a$. Prove that the number of solutions of $x^3\equiv a\pmod p$ equals $\sum_{\chi^3=\chi_0}\chi(a)$, the sum over characters mod $p$ whose cube is principal.
blocks.solution:
Let $g$ be a primitive root mod $p$ and $a\equiv g^e$. Characters mod $p$ are $\chi_k(g^j)=e^{2\pi ikj/(p-1)}$, and $\chi_k^3=\chi_0$ means $(p-1)\mid3k$.

Case $p\equiv2\pmod3$ (or $p=3$). Then $\gcd(3,p-1)=1$, so only $k=0$ qualifies and the sum is $1$. On the other side, $x\mapsto x^3$ is a bijection on $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, since $x^3\equiv y^3$ gives $(x/y)^3\equiv1$, and the order of $x/y$ divides $\gcd(3,p-1)=1$. So there is exactly one solution.

Case $p\equiv1\pmod3$. The qualifying $k$ are $0,\frac{p-1}3,\frac{2(p-1)}3$. So the sum is $\sum_{j=0}^2\omega^{je}$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, which is $3$ if $3\mid e$ and $0$ otherwise. On the other side, writing $x=g^y$, the congruence $x^3\equiv a$ becomes $3y\equiv e\pmod{p-1}$. This has $3$ solutions $y$ if $3\mid e$ and none otherwise. The counts agree.

The same argument shows that the number of solutions of $x^k\equiv a$ is $\sum_{\chi^k=\chi_0}\chi(a)$ for every $k$.

blocks.body:
- Orthogonality relation 3 needs $\gcd(a,q)=1$. If $\gcd(a,q)>1$, then $\overline\chi(a)=0$ for every $\chi$, and the left side is $0$ even for $n\equiv a$.
- $\chi_0$ mod $q$ is not the constant function $1$: it vanishes at integers sharing a factor with $q$. In particular $\chi_0$ mod $q$ is induced from the trivial character mod $1$, and is not primitive unless $q=1$.
- A character mod $q$ is a function on all of $\mathbb Z$. Do not forget the zeros when forming $L(s,\chi)=\sum\chi(n)n^{-s}$.
- Imprimitive and primitive versions of "the same" character have $L$-functions that differ by finitely many Euler factors $(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s})$ with $p\mid q$. This matters for functional equations and Gauss sums.
- Characters are not all real. For $q>2$ there are complex characters whenever $(\mathbb Z/q)^\times$ has an element of order greater than $2$.

Characters are the multiplicative side of Fourier analysis on $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$. The additive side is $e(an/q)$, and [[gauss-sums]] connect the two; for primitive $\chi$ they give $|g(\chi)|=\sqrt q$. Dirichlet $L$-functions $L(s,\chi)$ and the prime number theorem in progressions are developed in [[l-functions]], and the value $L(1,\chi)$ for real $\chi$ is given by the [[class-number-formula]]. Averages over all characters to many moduli are the subject of the [[large-sieve]]. Characters of order $3$ lead to [[cubic-characters]] and cubic reciprocity.

1. Show that the number of real characters mod $q$ equals the number of solutions of $x^2\equiv1\pmod q$. Compute it for $q=15$ and $q=16$.
2. Find all characters mod $7$, and identify which are even, which are odd, and which is the Legendre symbol.
3. Show that if $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ are primitive characters to coprime moduli $q_1,q_2$, then $\chi_1\chi_2$ is a primitive character mod $q_1q_2$.
4. Prove that $\sum_{\chi\bmod q}|\sum_{n\le N}\chi(n)|^2\le\varphi(q)\,N(N/q+1)$. (Expand the square and use orthogonality.)
